title: Preparing for the CCAF exam
tagline: Know the five CCAF exam domains, how questions are framed, and how to prepare.
summary: Hamza Farooq explains what the Claude Code Architect certification (CCAF) involves: who can sit it right now, the four free Anthropic Skilljar courses to finish first, and the five domains behind its 60 multiple-choice questions. Each domain gets a sample scenario question (duplicate charges after retries, tool misrouting, CLAUDE.md hierarchy, prompt injection, progressive summarization), alongside the Agent Architectures explainer from single skill to production agent. Hamza then demos a 5-minute quiz and a 55-question practice exam before taking attendee questions.

questions.q: What does the CCAF exam cover, and what is the format?
questions.answer:
The exam pulls from five domains [1]:

- agentic architecture and orchestration
- tool design and MCP integration
- Claude Code configuration and workflows
- prompt engineering and structured output
- context management and reliability

Hamza warns the questions are genuinely hard. As a data scientist rather than a full-stack developer, Hamza found CI/CD the toughest area [2]. Every question is multiple choice, 60 questions in 90 minutes as best Hamza recalls, and you do not need a Claude Code subscription to take the exam, only to use Claude Code itself [3].

citations.speaker: Hamza Farooq
citations.quote: there are 5 domains that they will test you on. They'll test you on agentic architecture and orchestration. Then they'll test you on tool design and MCP integration. … context management and reliability.

citations.speaker: Hamza Farooq
citations.quote: for me, the toughest part was CICD, because I'm more of a data scientist, I'm less of a full-stack developer.

citations.speaker: Hamza Farooq
citations.quote: you don't need Cloud Code subscription to take the exam. … all the questions are MCQ-style, 60 MCQ-style questions in 90 minutes, I think.

questions.q: Can I take the certification if my company isn't an Anthropic partner, and where should I start?
questions.answer:
Not yet, according to Hamza. Access runs through Anthropic's partner network, and the partner track and its interest form were paused at the time, with Hamza expecting individual registration to open in two to three weeks. If your company already works with Anthropic, your customer success contact can connect you [1].

While you wait, the courses are open to everyone:

- Sign up at anthropic.skilljar, register for the four courses in the learning path, and complete them in order [2].
- If you take only one, Hamza recommends Building with the Claude API, which took Hamza at least two hours and is still a regular reference [3].

Hamza says there are no real prerequisites beyond VS Code and GitHub.

citations.quote: your customer success agent, whoever is working with you, they can definitely connect you to the right people. … It's currently paused … But they are going to open it, I think, in 2-3 weeks

citations.quote: How to sign up, basically, is anthropic.skilljar. … Register for the four courses, which I've told you in the CPN Learning Path. complete them in order

questions.q: How do a skill, a subagent, an orchestrator and a production agent differ?
questions.answer:
Hamza uses the Agent Architectures explainer to show how deep the exam goes on agentic design. Each level builds on the last:

- **Single skill:** the starting point.
- **Subagent:** the work splits across a planner agent, a formatter and a research agent, with a human in the loop [1].
- **Orchestrator:** starts the process, sends information to individual agents, and a tech lead synthesizes what comes back [2].
- **Production agent:** a support agent with a pre-tool hook and a post-tool hook around its tools [3].

Hamza also stresses that subagents are stateless, so the full context has to be passed in the prompt [3]. Anthropic's course content covers each level.

citations.speaker: Hamza Farooq
citations.quote: you start with a skill, then there is sub-agent, where there is a human in the loop … there is a planner agent, there's a formatter, and there's a research agent.

citations.speaker: Hamza Farooq
citations.quote: So the orchestrator's job over here is basically, to sort of start with the process, and then send information to other pieces, to other individual agents, and then there is a tech lead … who's synthesizing everything

citations.speaker: Hamza Farooq
citations.quote: Sub-agents are stateless … they always pass the full context in the prompt … this is what a production agent looks like. You have a support agent … there's a pre-tool hook, there's a post-tool hook

questions.q: What does the practice quiz look like when Hamza runs it live?
questions.answer:
Hamza runs the short quiz live, about 10 questions meant to take five minutes. One question has a coordinator spawn six parallel agents, each researching a different competitor, with their outputs concatenated. The chat leaned toward C, and Hamza doubts that is right [1]. Pick a wrong option and the quiz explains why it is wrong and what the right answer would be [2].

For deeper prep there is a study guide covering each domain, then a practice exam of about 55 questions, with more to be added. The questions stay the same between attempts, so Hamza suggests taking the sample questions from the GitHub repo and having Claude build you a separate exam [3].

citations.speaker: Hamza Farooq
citations.quote: A coordinator spawns 6 parallel agents, each researching a different competitor, their outputs are concatenated. … So, Balaji, who says, C. … I don't think the answer is C

citations.speaker: Hamza Farooq
citations.quote: if you click on a wrong answer, it will just tell you why this answer is wrong, and, you know, why, what would be the right answer.

citations.speaker: Hamza Farooq
citations.quote: This exam has about, I think, 55 questions. I'll be adding more questions in the coming days … if you want to sort of build your own version, here's my GitHub. … Have Claude build you a separate exam.

questions.q: How should I approach the multiple-choice questions without falling for wrong answers?
questions.answer:
Hamza's personal method, offered as a recommendation rather than a rule, is to ignore the options at first and work out your own answer. It took Hamza longer, but an answer reached that way stuck [1].

Also learn to spot the distractors. Hamza lists the usual ones [2]:

- use a stronger system prompt
- use a larger model
- increase temperature
- add few-shot examples

Few-shot examples can be right in some use cases, but these options show up in almost every question, so Hamza treats them as a giveaway that they are not the fix [3].

citations.speaker: Hamza Farooq
citations.quote: my way of solving this exam, which I felt, you know, got me there, was… I did not look at what were the solution, what were the MCQ options. … But once I understood it, I would not forget it.

citations.speaker: Hamza Farooq
citations.quote: like, someone will say, use a stronger system prompt, so you… that's never the answer. Or use a larger model, that's never the answer. Increase temperature, or add a few short examples.

citations.speaker: Hamza Farooq
citations.quote: But it's an answer in some use cases. … you will see them almost in every question as a way to solve something, so it's a dead giveaway that they will not work for you
